Bhante, in 'web books meditations13 section0024 html 09b9e5' (web books meditations13 section0024 html 09b9e5), what is the core doctrinal teaching regarding 'The night before the Council, he'?

In this section from *web books meditations13 section0024 html 09b9e5*, the master explains: *"The night before the Council, he meditated very late into the night, practicing mindfulness immersed in the body."*. From the perspective of the Four Noble Truths, suffering arises whenever the mind grasps at impermanent phenomena (*anicca*) as a reliable self (*atta*). By establishing clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) and seeing conditioned events as empty of inherent ownership, craving (*taṇhā*) is unhooked. It is like grasping a poisonous cobra by the tail: tempting and sleek from afar, but deadly the moment you grasp it. Release the tail and live in safety. Anchor your understanding in direct seeing rather than speculative theory.

In sitting meditation, how do we work with the body and breath when 'web books meditations13 section0024 html 09b9e5' advises: 'The story of how he gained'?

The practical guidance given in *web books meditations13 section0024 html 09b9e5* instructs: *"The story of how he gained awakening is sometimes interpreted as meaning that he’d been trying too hard, he had too much desire—and when he gave up his desire, gave up his effort, that’s when he gained awakening."*. When you sit on the cushion, do not wage war against wandering thoughts. First ground attention in the physical posture—soften the belly, relax the face, and allow the breath to find its natural rhythm. When thoughts arise, notice the space around them rather than following the story. It is like still, flowing water (nam lai rin): awareness flows smoothly perceiving sights and sounds, while the heart inside remains utterly motionless. Rest the mind gently in the rhythm of each natural in-and-out breath.
